strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: extends tool-augmented, multi-step agentic reasoning (as popularized by ReAct/OpenThinkIMG-style frameworks) into the geospatial/EO domain, which prior EO-VLMs (GeoChat, EarthDial) and even recent EO-agent works (ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, Geo-OLM) only partially cover, as clearly summarized in Table 1.

Substantial, well-organized dataset (14,538 train / 1,169 eval instances, >100K/7K reasoning steps) spanning RGB, SAR, GIS vector layers, and spectral indices (NDVI/NBR/NDBI), with a described automated curation and validation pipeline (Sample Sufficiency Filter, Annotation Harmonizer, deterministic tool-call replay) that adds a degree of quality control beyond typical instruction-tuning corpora.

A concretely specified unified tool registry (Table A2) covering perceptual, GIS, spectral, georeferenced-raster, and utility operations with a consistent JSON-based calling schema, which is a useful engineering contribution for reproducible agentic pipelines.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation: both step-by-step (tool-agnostic) and end-to-end (live execution) protocols, multiple complementary metrics (Inst./Tool/ArgN/ArgV/Summ, category-wise F1, tool-order fidelity at three strictness levels, task accuracy), plus supplementary error-type breakdowns and a model-backbone ablation (Qwen3-4B vs Qwen2.5-7B).

The fine-tuned 4B model shows consistent, sizable improvements over its own untuned baseline and over much larger open-source models, and is competitive with or exceeds frontier proprietary models (GPT-4o, o4-mini) on several structural/procedural metrics (tool selection, argument correctness, trajectory-order fidelity), which is a meaningful applied result given the modest parameter count.
Illustrative qualitative examples (Figs. 1, A1-A3) make the intended use cases and failure modes of baselines concrete and support the paper's motivating claims.
weaknesses: The data-generation pipeline for natural-language queries and reasoning trajectories relies on an unspecified 'structured LLM-driven module'; the exact generator model(s), prompting strategy, and the extent/nature of human verification (beyond GSD sanity checks on the test set) are not clearly described, which limits reproducibility and raises questions about potential synthetic biases or repetitive patterns in the trajectories.

Methodologically the core training contribution is standard supervised fine-tuning on curated trajectories (Eq. 2-3); the technical novelty is concentrated in dataset construction and tool-registry engineering rather than in the learning algorithm itself, which should be more explicitly framed (the paper is best read as a Dataset/Benchmark + Applied/Systems contribution rather than a new algorithmic method).

Several evaluation category subsets are small (e.g., only 123 index-based and 503 RGB/SAR queries in the 1,169-sample benchmark), which may limit the statistical robustness of category-wise comparisons (Fig. 7) and some F1 breakdowns.

Precise operational definitions of some metrics (e.g., exactly how Instance Accuracy or Summarization Accuracy are computed, and how the LLM-judge prompt in Fig. A5 handles edge cases beyond the examples shown) are only partially specified; combined with use of an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) for non-generative task accuracy, this introduces potential evaluation noise/bias that is not quantified (e.g., no inter-rater or judge-consistency check).

No explicit statement of dataset/code release, licensing of the underlying source datasets for redistribution (DOTA, xBD, FloodNet, OSM, GEE, etc.), or compute/training-run variance (single run, no seeds/repeats reported), which affects reproducibility claims.

Comparisons to frontier closed models (GPT-4o, o4-mini) are somewhat asymmetric since those models are not fine-tuned on the target distribution, so some of OpenEarthAgent's gains may partly reflect in-domain adaptation rather than a more general reasoning improvement; this should be discussed as a caveat.
Minor presentation issues remain, e.g., a broken cross-reference ('Table ??') in the Data Sources paragraph, indicating incomplete proofreading.

strengths: Introduces a reasonably large-scale, multi-domain dataset (14,538 train / 1,169 eval instances, >100K reasoning steps) linking imagery (optical, SAR, GIS, multispectral indices) with explicit multi-step thought-action-observation trajectories, which is a useful resource for the understudied intersection of GIS reasoning and remote-sensing VLMs.

The unified tool registry (perceptual, GIS, spectral, georeferenced raster, utility tools) with a consistent callable schema is a sensible engineering contribution that supports extensibility without retraining.

Empirical results show that a small 4B fine-tuned model can match or exceed much larger open-source models and approach/exceed closed frontier models on several step-by-step and end-to-end metrics, suggesting the curated trajectories are informative for training.
The paper includes fairly detailed supplementary material (error-type analysis, model-selection ablation, tool I/O schema, evaluation prompt) that adds some transparency to the evaluation protocol.

Addresses a legitimate gap: existing EO foundation models and VLMs are largely single-pass/perception-centric, and prior EO agent works (ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, Geo-OLM) are noted to rely on predefined workflows or prompt heuristics rather than learned, verifiable multi-step policies.
weaknesses: Evaluation is conducted entirely on the authors' own curated benchmark; there is no evaluation on independent, previously published EO-agent benchmarks (e.g., ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent) despite these being discussed at length as the most directly comparable prior work, making claims of 'competitive performance' hard to verify and raising concern about distributional overlap between train/test splits generated by the same pipeline.

Methodological novelty is limited: the approach is standard supervised fine-tuning (next-token MLE) on validated tool-call trajectories; no exploration of reinforcement learning or verification-in-the-loop training is attempted, despite the related-work discussion emphasizing RL-based tool-use methods (VisTA, OpenThinkIMG, DeepEyes) as the current frontier.

Dataset quality control is described loosely ('controlled regeneration and targeted manual verification when necessary'); the extent and rigor of human verification (e.g., inter-annotator agreement, sample size manually checked) is not quantified, and reasoning traces/queries are LLM-synthesized from templates, raising concerns about diversity and potential artifacts/bias inherited from the generating LLM.

The LLM-judge (gpt-4o-mini) used for non-generation task accuracy introduces potential evaluation bias/circularity, and no human-verification or agreement study of the judge's reliability is reported.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: OpenEarthAgent underperforms GPT-4o on image-generation success (75.86 vs 77.93) and on GIS-based category score vs itself inconsistently framed; the paper's narrative emphasizes favorable comparisons while downplaying cases where frontier models remain stronger (e.g., Summarization Accuracy, GIS F1 nuances).
Minor but indicative polish issues include an unresolved cross-reference ('Table ??') and duplicated sentences (batch size of 16 stated twice), suggesting incomplete proofreading.
No analysis of generalization to out-of-distribution geospatial regions/tasks beyond the held-out split drawn from the same curation pipeline, limiting confidence in broader applicability claims.

Licensing/attribution details for the many aggregated third-party datasets (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, FloodNet, etc.) and OSM/GEE-derived content are not discussed, which is relevant for a dataset contribution intended for release and reuse.

strengths: Introduces a large, well-structured multimodal corpus (14,538 train / 1,169 eval instances, >100K reasoning steps) that explicitly pairs satellite imagery, natural-language queries, and multi-step tool-use reasoning traces spanning RGB, SAR, GIS, and spectral-index (NDVI/NBR/NDBI) modalities, filling a genuine gap relative to prior perception-only EO benchmarks and prior EO agent work (ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent, Geo-OLM).

The automated curation pipeline (sufficiency filtering, annotation harmonization, deterministic tool-call replay for verification, manual test-set inspection) is reasonably well described and adds credibility to data quality/correctness.

A unified, extensible tool registry (perceptual, GIS, spectral, georeferenced-raster, utility tools) with standardized JSON I/O schemas is a practically useful contribution for reproducibility and future tool integration.

Extensive empirical evaluation under both step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, against a broad set of frontier (GPT-4o, o4-mini) and open-source baselines (Qwen, Llama, InternLM, Mistral), with fine-grained metrics (tool selection F1 by category, trajectory order fidelity, argument accuracy) rather than a single aggregate score.

Despite using only a 4B backbone, OpenEarthAgent achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive results on most structural/procedural metrics (Inst./Tool/ArgN/ArgV, trajectory order accuracy) versus much larger and proprietary models, and the supplementary error analysis and model-selection ablation add useful evidence of the training approach's efficacy.
Qualitative examples (Fig. 1, supplementary Figs. A1-A3) clearly illustrate the practical value of structured tool orchestration over free-form baseline reasoning, improving interpretability.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is primarily supervised fine-tuning of an existing ReAct-style tool-agent formulation on a new dataset; there is no new architectural or algorithmic mechanism beyond standard trajectory-level SFT with masked tool observations, so novelty rests almost entirely on the dataset/pipeline rather than the learning method.

Task/modality distribution in the dataset is heavily skewed toward RGB/SAR perceptual queries (10,670/14,538 train, ~73%) versus GIS (3,645) and especially index-based queries (223), which may limit the claimed breadth of 'index-driven' reasoning coverage and could bias reported gains toward perceptual tasks.

Despite strong procedural/tool-selection metrics, overall end-to-end task accuracy remains modest in absolute terms (Ans. 45.26% even for the proposed model), indicating that correct tool orchestration does not fully translate into correct final answers; this gap between procedural fidelity and task correctness is not deeply analyzed.

Final answer/task correctness evaluation relies on an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) with a single prompt template; no inter-rater agreement, human verification of judge reliability, or sensitivity analysis is reported, which is a concern given LLM-judge biases are well documented.

The paper reuses many third-party datasets (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, AID, NWPU-VHR-10, FloodNet, Global-Dumpsite, SAR datasets, OSM, GEE) to construct the corpus, but licensing/redistribution terms and attribution details for the derived/merged dataset are not discussed, which matters for reproducibility and release.
Minor presentation issues remain (e.g., a broken cross-reference 'Table ??' in Section 3), suggesting the manuscript could benefit from another proofreading pass.

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported for the single-run SFT experiments, and no ablations isolate the effect of dataset scale, task-type balance, or specific pipeline components (e.g., validation/replay step) on downstream performance.

strengths: Comprehensive multimodal corpus (14,538 train / 1,169 test instances, 100K+ reasoning steps) spanning RGB, SAR, GIS, and spectral-index modalities across seven thematic domains, filling a genuine gap relative to prior EO benchmarks that largely lack explicit tool-grounded reasoning traces.

Well-engineered data curation pipeline with deterministic replay validation (executing candidate tool calls to verify argument correctness and geometric validity before inclusion), which is a meaningful step toward higher-quality supervision than purely LLM-generated trajectories.

Extensive empirical evaluation: both step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, comparison against a wide range of frontier (GPT-5, GPT-4o, o4-mini) and open-source baselines, plus a large supplementary suite of ablations (data composition, in-context learning vs. fine-tuning, tool-schema complexity, tool ordering, high-level planning, cross-benchmark evaluation on Earth-Agent, and LLM-judge robustness checks).

Demonstrates that a small (4B) fine-tuned model can match or exceed much larger frontier models on procedural correctness metrics (Inst./Tool/ArgN/ArgV) and trajectory-order fidelity, which is a practically useful and interesting finding for resource-constrained deployment.
Clear, modular tool-registry abstraction (perceptual, GIS, spectral, georeferenced-raster, utility tools) that is extensible without retraining, supporting reproducibility and reuse.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is primarily supervised fine-tuning on a curated trajectory corpus with a standardized tool schema; there is limited architectural or algorithmic novelty beyond this (no RL, no novel policy-learning mechanism), which somewhat narrows the technical contribution relative to the claims of a "unified agentic architecture."

Both the training data (queries + reasoning traces) and much of the evaluation (Summarization/Answer Accuracy via GPT-4o-mini as judge) are LLM-generated/LLM-judged, raising potential circularity and reliability concerns; the Qwen3-30B judge comparison helps but only shows rank preservation, not absolute calibration against human judgment beyond the test-set manual inspection.

Table 4 GIS F1 scores are near-saturated (>90%) for nearly all models including weak baselines, which is suspicious and suggests the GIS tool-selection task may be too easy/low-diversity to be discriminative, undermining the strength of claims about superior GIS reasoning.

No direct comparison against the actual Earth-Agent or ThinkGeo systems (only their backbone LLMs are compared within the authors' own framework), so it is unclear how OpenEarthAgent performs against these prior tool-augmented EO agents' own pipelines rather than re-implemented baselines.

The underlying imagery/annotation sources (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, etc.) are pre-existing benchmarks; the novelty rests on the synthesized queries/reasoning traces layered on top, and the paper does not discuss potential biases or artifacts introduced by the LLM-driven question/trace synthesis pipeline (e.g., template diversity, hallucinated reasoning steps that still execute correctly).

Limited discussion of failure cases or limitations of the approach itself (e.g., generalization to truly out-of-distribution geospatial tasks, tool registry scalability, robustness to real GIS/GeoTIFF edge cases) in the main text; most of this appears only in supplementary error analysis.

strengths: The paper tackles an underexplored problem: coupling tool-augmented agentic reasoning with earth observation data across optical, SAR, GIS-vector, and spectral-index modalities in a single unified tool registry/schema, which is a reasonable and useful engineering contribution.

The dataset construction pipeline is comprehensive, pulling from many public RS sources (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, FloodNet, OSM, GEE indices) and includes a deterministic replay/validation step intended to guarantee executability of reasoning trajectories, which is a sound idea for reducing hallucinated tool calls.

The experimental section is extensive: step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, F1 by tool category, tool-order fidelity metrics, and a long list of ablations in the supplementary (data composition, in-context learning, tool-schema verbosity, tool ordering, high-level planning, model-size selection, cross-benchmark transfer to Earth-Agent, error-type breakdown, domain-stratified performance, and LLM-judge robustness check).

The fine-tuned 4B model shows clear, consistent gains over its own un-tuned baseline (Qwen3-4B-Instruct) and over similarly sized or larger open-source models on procedural correctness metrics (tool selection, argument validity, tool-order fidelity), suggesting the trajectory-supervised fine-tuning approach has practical value for smaller deployable models.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'competitive performance against recent open and closed-source models' is weaker than advertised on the metric that matters most (final task correctness): in Table 3, OpenEarthAgent's Summarization accuracy (83.64) still trails gpt-4o (86.76) and o4-mini (89.48); in Table 4, GPT-4o still leads on image-generation accuracy. The paper's narrative emphasizes procedural metrics (tool/argument correctness, tool-order fidelity) where OpenEarthAgent wins, but these are proxies that do not fully establish that end-task reasoning quality has caught up to frontier models.

The entire training and evaluation corpus is synthetically generated via an LLM-driven question/trajectory synthesizer with only automated (and, for test-only, limited manual) validation. Validation checks executability and argument correctness, not whether the generated queries are realistic, diverse, or representative of genuine downstream GIS/EO use cases; this raises concerns about dataset quality, distributional artifacts, and possible shortcut learning by the fine-tuned model on its own generator's style.

Final-answer correctness is scored by an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini, with a secondary check using Qwen3-30B in the supplement). While a consistency check is provided, this does not establish absolute reliability of the judge, and LLM-judged accuracy for a method whose training data was also synthesized by LLMs raises circularity/self-consistency concerns that are not discussed.

No discussion of train/test overlap or leakage control across the many underlying source datasets (DOTA, DIOR, xBD, etc.) and across the LLM-driven query generation pipeline; given the same generation pipeline is used for both splits, there is a non-trivial risk of distributional leakage inflating the fine-tuned model's apparent advantage.

Methodological novelty is modest: the core technique is standard supervised fine-tuning on ReAct-style thought-action-observation trajectories (Eq. 1–3), essentially replicating prior tool-augmented agent training recipes (e.g., OpenThinkIMG) adapted to EO tools. The tool-schema ablation (Table A3) shows that most of the gain comes from prompt/schema engineering (providing full JSON examples) rather than from any new architectural or algorithmic idea, undercutting the paper's framing as a new 'agentic architecture.'

Several ablations and comparisons are run as single experiments without repeated trials, confidence intervals, or variance estimates, making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., +1-2 points in F1) are meaningful or within noise.

The qualitative comparison in Fig. 1 is a single cherry-picked example contrasting OpenEarthAgent with the untuned Qwen3-4B baseline; such anecdotal evidence is presented prominently in the main text but does not substitute for broader statistical evidence of the claimed reasoning-robustness gap.
Code and trained models are stated as 'will be publicly available' rather than being released with the submission, limiting independent verification of reproducibility at review time.

The paper provides no discussion of limitations (e.g., reliance on synthetic data, judge-based evaluation, generalization to truly out-of-distribution geographies/sensors beyond the Earth-Agent cross-benchmark) or of societal impact/dual-use considerations relevant to geospatial agentic tooling (e.g., misuse for surveillance), which would have strengthened the submission's completeness.

strengths: Presents a comprehensive, large-scale multimodal corpus (14,538 train / 1,169 test instances, >107K reasoning steps) spanning RGB, SAR, GIS, and spectral-index (NDVI/NBR/NDBI) modalities across seven thematic domains, filling a genuine gap between GIS analysis tools and remote-sensing perception models.

The unified tool registry with a standardized JSON-based executable schema and deterministic replay validation is a solid engineering contribution that enables reproducible, verifiable multi-step reasoning chains rather than free-form text generation.

Extensive experimental evaluation with two complementary protocols (step-by-step and end-to-end), fine-grained metrics (Inst./Tool./ArgN./ArgV./Summ., per-category F1, tool-order fidelity), and comparisons against a wide range of frontier (GPT-5, GPT-4o, o4-mini) and open-source baselines.

Strong empirical results: a 4B fine-tuned model is competitive with or exceeds much larger proprietary models on several structural/tool-fidelity metrics and shows the largest gains in tool-order consistency, suggesting the value of trajectory-based supervised alignment over model scale alone.

Rich supplementary material with numerous informative ablations (data composition/difficulty, in-context learning comparison, tool schema information content, tool ordering, high-level planning, base-model selection, error-type analysis, domain-stratified performance, and cross-benchmark evaluation on Earth-Agent), which substantially strengthens the empirical case and provides useful insights for practitioners.

Cross-judge robustness check (GPT-4o-mini vs. Qwen3-30B) for the LLM-based answer scoring shows consistent relative model rankings despite absolute score shifts, partially addressing evaluation-metric reliability concerns.
Clear, well-illustrated qualitative examples (Figs. 1, A3–A5) that make the agentic workflow and tool orchestration process interpretable.
weaknesses: The dataset construction pipeline (question synthesis, reasoning-trace generation) and the primary evaluation judge both rely heavily on LLMs (including GPT family models), raising potential circularity/self-consistency concerns when benchmarking against GPT-family baselines; no validation against human annotator agreement is reported for either the training traces or the LLM-judge scores.

Absolute end-to-end Answer accuracy remains fairly low across all models (best is 45.26%), and the paper does not fully contextualize how much headroom exists or what failure modes underlie this gap beyond the qualitative error taxonomy, tempering claims of practical readiness for real-world EO decision-making.

Details of the automated curation/quality-control pipeline (e.g., criteria and extent of 'targeted manual verification,' inter-annotator checks, exact filtering thresholds) are somewhat underspecified, making full reproducibility of dataset quality difficult to assess.

The model-selection and generalization ablations are limited to variants of the Qwen family; it is unclear how well the framework and training recipe transfer to other backbone architectures or larger context/step budgets.
Code, dataset, and trained models are stated as 'will be publicly available' rather than already released, so reviewers/readers cannot yet verify reproducibility claims at submission time.

The step-by-step evaluation mode (used for Table 3) does not execute tools and thus may not fully capture compounding/error-propagation effects that occur in real deployment, partially limiting the interpretive strength of those state-of-the-art claims relative to the more informative end-to-end results.
